title: Embeddings and Semantic Search
summary: Embeddings turn text into vectors that capture meaning, so semantically similar texts have similar vectors. Semantic search finds relevant documents by vector similarity rather than exact keywords. This is the retrieval engine behind RAG, the most co
content:
# Embeddings and Semantic Search ##### The chunk that split a sentence in half A team in Ahmedabad built semantic search over their insurance policy documents. Retrieval quality was inconsistent in a way they could not pin down — some questions worked perfectly, others returned confidently irrelevant paragraphs. They eventually printed the chunks themselves. One read: > "...the policyholder is not entitled to claim reimbursement for treatments undertaken" The next chunk began: > "outside the network hospital list, unless prior authorisation was obtained." Their fixed-size splitter had cut at exactly 500 characters, mid-sentence, right at the clause that inverted the meaning. Chunk one, read alone, says claims are not reimbursable. Chunk two, read alone, is a fragment. Neither is retrievable as an answer to "can I claim for treatment at a non-network hospital?" — and when chunk one *was* retrieved, the LLM confidently gave the wrong answer. They changed one parameter: `chunk_overlap` from 0 to 150. Retrieval accuracy on their test set went from 62% to 88%. **Chunking is the most underrated part of a retrieval system.** Everyone tunes the embedding model and the top-k; almost nobody looks at their actual chunks. Today covers both — and the chunk inspection habit is the one that will save you most often. ##### Embedding models Day 20 gave you static word embeddings: one vector per word. Modern embedding models produce **one vector per piece of text**, contextually computed. The key architectural insight comes from Sentence-BERT (Reimers & Gurevych, 2019). Plain BERT can compare two sentences, but only by running both through the model together — which means comparing one query against 10,000 documents needs 10,000 forward passes. Sentence-BERT uses a **siamese** setup: encode each text independently into a fixed vector, then compare with cosine similarity. Now you embed your corpus once and every query is a single forward pass plus a matrix multiply. That change took semantic search from 65 hours to about 5 seconds for a 10,000-document corpus. ```python from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer import numpy as np model = SentenceTransformer("all-MiniLM-L6-v2") texts = [ "How do I claim reimbursement for hospital treatment?", "What is the process for getting medical expenses refunded?", "How do I update my GSTIN on the invoice?", ] emb = model.encode(texts, normalize_embeddings=True) print(emb.shape) # (3, 384) sims = emb @ emb.T # cosine, since normalised print(sims.round(3)) # [[1.000 0.847 0.212] # [0.847 1.000 0.198] # [0.212 0.198 1.000]] ``` 0.847 between two sentences that share almost no words. That is the whole value proposition — and it is precisely what TF-IDF from Day 19 could never do. **Choosing a model:** | Model | Dims | Speed | Notes | |---|---|---|---| | `all-MiniLM-L6-v2` | 384 | Very fast | **Best default for learning**; runs on CPU | | `all-mpnet-base-v2` | 768 | Moderate | Better quality, still local | | `BAAI/bge-base-en-v1.5` | 768 | Moderate | Strong on MTEB benchmarks | | `intfloat/multilingual-e5-base` | 768 | Moderate | **Multilingual, good for Indic** | | OpenAI `text-embedding-3-small` | 1536 | API | Cheap, strong, no local compute | | OpenAI `text-embedding-3-large` | 3072 | API | Best quality, higher cost | Check the **MTEB leaderboard** on Hugging Face for current rankings, but do not chase the top spot blindly. A 384-dimension model that runs on CPU at 2,000 texts/second may beat a 3072-dimension API model once you account for cost, latency, and storage. **Two rules that catch people out:** 1. **Query and documents must use the same model.** Vectors from different models are not comparable at all — the similarity numbers will be meaningless, not merely worse. 2. **Some models need prefixes.** E5 and BGE models are trained with `"query: "` and `"passage: "` prefixes, and omitting them costs several points of accuracy. ```python model = SentenceTransformer("intfloat/multilingual-e5-base") q = model.encode("query: कैसे क्लेम करें?", normalize_embeddings=True) d = model.encode(["passage: क्लेम के लिए फॉर्म भरें..."], normalize_embeddings=True) ``` ##### Cosine similarity From Day 6, applied: $$\text{cos}(a, b) = \frac{a \cdot b}{\|a\| \|b\|}$$ If you normalise vectors to unit length first, cosine similarity *is* the dot product — so the whole search reduces to one matrix multiplication. ```python import numpy as np def semantic_search(query, doc_embeddings, docs, model, k=5): q = model.encode([query], normalize_embeddings=True)[0] scores = doc_embeddings @ q # (n_docs,) top = np.argsort(-scores)[:k] return [(docs[i], float(scores[i])) for i in top] ``` **Cosine vs Euclidean vs dot product:** for normalised vectors, cosine similarity and Euclidean distance rank identically, so the choice does not matter. For unnormalised vectors, dot product favours longer vectors (which can be useful if magnitude encodes something) while cosine ignores magnitude entirely. **Normalise and use cosine** unless you have a specific reason not to. Rough interpretation of scores, though it varies by model: | Cosine | Meaning | |---|---| | > 0.85 | Near-duplicate or direct paraphrase | | 0.65–0.85 | Strongly related | | 0.45–0.65 | Loosely related, same topic | | < 0.35 | Unrelated | Do not hardcode a threshold across models. Calibrate on your own data — many models produce a compressed range where even unrelated text scores 0.5. ##### Chunking strategies Documents are too long to embed whole. A 40-page policy PDF becomes one vector that means nothing in particular. You must split — and *how* you split determines retrieval quality more than any other choice. ```mermaid flowchart TD A["Raw document"] --> B{"Chunking strategy"} B --> C["Fixed size
split every N chars"] B --> D["Recursive
try paragraph, then
sentence, then char"] B --> E["Semantic
split where meaning
shifts"] B --> F["Structural
by heading, section,
or table"] C --> G["Fast, simple,
breaks sentences ✗"] D --> H["Good default ✓"] E --> I["Best quality,
slow and costly"] F --> J["Best for structured
docs ✓"] ``` ```python from langchain_text_splitters import (RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter, MarkdownHeaderTextSplitter) # The sensible default splitter = RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter( chunk_size=800, chunk_overlap=150, # ← the Ahmedabad fix separators=["\n\n", "\n", ". ", "? ", "! ", " ", ""], length_function=len, ) chunks = splitter.split_documents(docs) # For structured markdown, split by heading first md_splitter = MarkdownHeaderTextSplitter( headers_to_split_on=[("#", "h1"), ("##", "h2"), ("###", "h3")] ) sections = md_splitter.split_text(markdown_text) # then apply the recursive splitter within each section ``` **Choosing chunk size:** | Size | Good for | Risk | |---|---|---| | 200–400 chars | Precise fact lookup, FAQs | Loses surrounding context | | **500–1000** | **General purpose — start here** | — | | 1500–2500 | Narrative, reasoning over passages | Dilutes the embedding; retrieval gets fuzzy | | Whole document | Very short docs only | One vector cannot represent many topics | **Overlap should be 10–20% of chunk size.** It costs storage and creates near-duplicate results, but it means a concept that straddles a boundary appears intact in at least one chunk. Zero overlap is the single most common chunking mistake. **Always attach metadata**, because it is what makes filtering possible tomorrow: ```python for i, chunk in enumerate(chunks): chunk.metadata.update({ "chunk_id": i, "source": chunk.metadata.get("source"), "page": chunk.metadata.get("page"), "section": detect_section(chunk.page_content), "n_chars": len(chunk.page_content), "ingested_at": "2026-07-29", }) ``` **And inspect your chunks.** Print twenty random ones and read them. If any starts mid-sentence or contains only a table header, your splitter needs work. This five-minute check would have saved Ahmedabad three weeks. ##### Semantic vs keyword search Neither one dominates. They fail differently. | | Keyword (BM25) | Semantic (embeddings) | |---|---|---| | Synonyms | ✗ misses entirely | ✓ handles well | | Exact IDs, codes, SKUs | ✓ exact match | ✗ often misses | | Rare technical terms | ✓ | ✗ may not be in training | | Paraphrased queries | ✗ | ✓ | | Typos | ✗ | ✓ tolerant | | Explainability | ✓ you see the matched terms | ✗ opaque | | Cost | Very low | Embedding + storage | The classic semantic failure: searching for invoice `INV-2024-88231`. That string means nothing semantically, so the embedding is close to nothing. BM25 finds it instantly. The classic keyword failure: "stomach ache" against a corpus that says "abdominal pain" — Day 20's example. **The answer is hybrid search**, which Day 36 covers in detail. For now, know that production systems run both and fuse the results, typically with Reciprocal Rank Fusion. ##### A complete semantic search engine ```python import numpy as np from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer from langchain_text_splitters import RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter class SemanticSearch: def __init__(self, model_name="all-MiniLM-L6-v2", chunk_size=800, chunk_overlap=150): self.model = SentenceTransformer(model_name) self.splitter = RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter( chunk_size=chunk_size, chunk_overlap=chunk_overlap, separators=["\n\n", "\n", ". ", " ", ""], ) self.chunks: list[str] = [] self.metadata: list[dict] = [] self.embeddings: np.ndarray | None = None def add_documents(self, documents: list[dict]): """documents: [{'text': ..., 'source': ..., ...}]""" for doc in documents: pieces = self.splitter.split_text(doc["text"]) for i, piece in enumerate(pieces): self.chunks.append(piece) meta = {k: v for k, v in doc.items() if k != "text"} meta.update({"chunk_index": i, "n_chars": len(piece)}) self.metadata.append(meta) self._reindex() def _reindex(self): self.embeddings = self.model.encode( self.chunks, normalize_embeddings=True, batch_size=64, show_progress_bar=True, ) def search(self, query: str, k: int = 5, min_score: float = 0.0): q = self.model.encode([query], normalize_embeddings=True)[0] scores = self.embeddings @ q top = np.argsort(-scores)[:k] return [ {"text": self.chunks[i], "score": float(scores[i]), "metadata": self.metadata[i]} for i in top if scores[i] >= min_score ] engine = SemanticSearch() engine.add_documents([ {"text": open("policy.txt").read(), "source": "policy.txt", "year": 2026}, ]) for hit in engine.search("Can I claim treatment at a non-network hospital?", k=3): print(f"[{hit['score']:.3f}] {hit['text'][:140]}...") ``` That is a working semantic search engine in about fifty lines. Tomorrow you replace the brute-force `@` with an ANN index and add persistence. ##### Evaluating retrieval You cannot improve what you do not measure, and "it seems better" is not measurement. **Build a small evaluation set.** Twenty to fifty queries with the chunk IDs that *should* be retrieved. Writing these by hand is tedious and it is the highest-value hour you will spend on the project. ```python def evaluate_retrieval(engine, eval_set, k=5): """eval_set: [{'query': str, 'relevant_ids': set[int]}]""" recalls, mrrs, precisions = [], [], [] for item in eval_set: hits = engine.search(item["query"], k=k) retrieved = [h["metadata"]["chunk_index"] for h in hits] relevant = item["relevant_ids"] found = set(retrieved) & relevant recalls.append(len(found) / len(relevant) if relevant else 0.0) precisions.append(len(found) / k) rr = 0.0 for rank, cid in enumerate(retrieved, start=1): if cid in relevant: rr = 1.0 / rank break mrrs.append(rr) return { f"recall@{k}": round(sum(recalls) / len(recalls), 3), f"precision@{k}": round(sum(precisions) / len(precisions), 3), "MRR": round(sum(mrrs) / len(mrrs), 3), } ``` **The metrics that matter:** - **Recall@k** — did the right chunk make it into the top k? For RAG this is the critical one: if the answer is not retrieved, the LLM cannot possibly produce it. - **MRR** — how high did the first relevant result rank? Matters because LLMs attend more to earlier context. - **Precision@k** — how much of what you retrieved was useful? Low precision wastes context tokens. **Prioritise recall over precision in RAG.** A reranker (Day 36) can filter out irrelevant chunks from a larger candidate set, but nothing can recover a chunk that was never retrieved. ##### Common mistakes - **`chunk_overlap=0`**, splitting sentences and clauses — the Ahmedabad bug. - **Never reading your actual chunks.** - **Different embedding models for queries and documents.** - **Forgetting E5/BGE query and passage prefixes.** - **Not normalising vectors** before treating dot product as cosine. - **Chunks too large**, so one vector tries to represent five topics. - **No metadata**, making filtering impossible later. - **Hardcoding a similarity threshold** across different models. - **Semantic search alone for IDs, SKUs, and error codes** — use hybrid. - **No evaluation set**, so every change is a guess. - **Re-embedding the entire corpus** on every startup instead of persisting. - **Optimising precision when recall is the binding constraint** for RAG. ##### Hands-on: measure your chunking Your practical task embeds documents and retrieves top-k by cosine similarity. Use the `SemanticSearch` class above. Then do the thing most people skip: print the top-3 chunks for five real queries and read them. You will immediately see whether your chunks are coherent units or arbitrary fragments, and that observation will drive your next change. The mini project builds a search engine with adjustable chunking and top-k. Make chunk size and overlap constructor arguments so you can rebuild the index quickly — that adjustability is what makes the assignment tractable. Add a small CLI or Streamlit UI showing the score and source for each result; seeing scores next to results teaches you your model's calibration faster than any table. The assignment tests three chunk sizes against retrieval quality. Use 300, 800, and 2000 characters with proportional overlap, and evaluate all three on the same 20-query set with the function above. Report recall@5 and MRR for each. The typical result — mid-size winning, small chunks losing context, large chunks diluting the embedding — is worth confirming yourself, because the *right* size depends on your documents, and now you know how to find it. ##### Key takeaways - **Sentence embeddings encode each text independently**, which is what makes searching 10,000 documents a single matrix multiply rather than 10,000 forward passes. - **Chunking determines retrieval quality more than model choice.** Use recursive splitting, 500–1000 characters, and 10–20% overlap — and read your chunks. - **Query and document embeddings must come from the same model**, with the same prefixes if the model expects them. - **Semantic and keyword search fail differently** — synonyms versus exact IDs — which is why production systems run both. - **Build a 20–50 query evaluation set and optimise recall@k**, because a reranker can filter noise but nothing recovers a chunk that was never retrieved.
practical_task_reference: Embed a set of documents, then given a query, retrieve the top-k most similar using cosine similarity.
mini_project_reference: Build a semantic search engine over a collection of articles with adjustable chunking and top-k retrieval.
assignment_reference: Experiment with three chunk sizes and measure their effect on retrieval quality for sample queries.
